text: AI agents are starting to earn money, and each one answers to a single owner. Koperasi gives an agent to a co-op: its members own it, one vote each, and every rule lives on NEAR.

This is the live page. Your browser reads all of it from NEAR testnet. The first panel asks: who controls this agent? The members vote, one each. Its instructions are locked in by-laws, version ten right now. And the agent obeys. Hand it any other version and it stops.
The hackathon's Social Money brief is checked the same way. Collective ownership, a shared budget, programmable rewards, and access by reputation. Each line is read from the chain as the page loads.

Don't trust us. Your browser checks. This button asks NEAR AI Cloud to prove its model runs in an Intel TDX enclave, bound to a nonce my browser just made. Meanwhile, the page hashes the by-laws and matches them to the members' vote. The contract has no full-access key, so only a vote changes its code. Nineteen attacks were refused on-chain. And the answer is back: Intel TDX, up to date, bound to my nonce.

The agent's work leaves receipts. On Taskbond, another team's testnet market, it won six jobs, and that market's reviewer scored them ninety-five out of a hundred four times, and eighty-five twice. Every paid job records its price, its inference cost, the by-laws it ran under, and its TEE proof.

The agent can also propose changes to its own by-laws. It read its record in a TEE and proposed version nine, with a lower price, and the members approved. But version nine rested on a wrong average: it counted a job paid in testnet NEAR as zero dollars. So the members put version eight's terms back, as version ten. The agent proposes. The members decide.

And when the agent gets a job wrong, it pays. A buyer's dispute goes to a jury of three members. If two uphold it, the buyer is refunded at once, from a risk fund the agent saves into. Each upheld case halves the agent's share of the surplus. At three cases, the contract suspends it.

A second worker runs as a Shade Agent. Its key was made inside an Intel TDX virtual machine. A registry owned by the co-op's DAO verified its attestation on-chain, after the members approved its code and its machine by vote. Then it recorded a receipt from inside the TEE.

Co-ops can also join together. Their federation's loan ceiling is enforced by the contract: when these members voted for four percent loans, the contract refused. And a member's record at a sister co-op counts as credit here.
On the co-ops page, every resolution was cast by each co-op's own vote, including one that lets their agents pass work to each other.

Inside the co-op, each member has one vote. Small tasks pay out on earned trust, after a ten-minute window for any member to veto. Profit is shared by a rule the members voted. And standing comes from pledges kept and jury duty served.
Every member has a work record, read live from the chain. Type an account, and you see their pledges and jury duty. Nobody can type the record itself.
Members work in their own app. Open it from the page.
The overview shows the co-op at a glance. The agent's view puts its by-laws, the Shade Agent and its receipts side by side.

And this is what a member sees, here as Bob. First, what needs his vote. Type an amount for a profit share, and every member's part shows before anyone votes. Below that are the tasks he can take, each with what it pays. Then the pledges other members made, which he can call in. And surety: standing behind another member's loan. The app also speaks Bahasa Indonesia.

The agent report judges the agent like a member. In court, nine of its thirteen cases were upheld. Three strikes suspended it once, and the members reinstated it. To come back, it filed a recovery plan, which the members approved, pinned by its hash. Its share restarts at a quarter and climbs back over thirty days.

Between co-ops, the agent posts jobs below its price to a sister co-op, and the sister's own contract shows it accepted one. The members can also lend from the risk fund to a sister co-op, by vote. This loan came back in full, with five cents of interest.

Juries are drawn by reputation, square-root weighted, so no single member can capture one. And technical polls are weighed by reputation too, as the members chose by vote. In this one, the larger model won, two hundred eighty to two hundred twenty.
You don't have to trust this video either. One command reads every claim from the chain, with no keys and no transactions. Ninety-five claims, and every one checks out.
Koperasi. The members own the agent, and the chain keeps the receipts.
